title: Germany Money Flow Atlas
live_note: The dashboard uses the latest verified public snapshot and attempts to refresh selected ECB wealth series in the browser. It is not a feed of private bank transactions.

sources.title: Net wealth of households — total
supports: Adjusted household net wealth of approximately €19.918 trillion in Q4 2025.
sources.does_not_prove: The identity of individual wealthy households or the liquidity of their assets.

sources.title: Share of net wealth held by top 10%
supports: The top 10% held 59.48% of adjusted household net wealth.
sources.does_not_prove: That every household in the top decile is equally wealthy or that all wealth could be taxed or transferred without behavioural effects.

sources.title: Net wealth of bottom 50%
supports: The bottom 50% held approximately €431.9 billion of adjusted household net wealth.
Against the total series this is about 2.17%.
sources.does_not_prove: Individual household hardship; net wealth and disposable income measure different things.

sources.title: Household financial assets and real returns
sources.exact_location: 16 July 2026 release · household financial assets and DWA return analysis
supports: Household financial assets were €9.490 trillion at end-Q1 2026.
Average real financial-asset returns remained positive only for the wealthiest 10% in that quarter.
The less wealthy half holds financial assets mostly as deposits and insurance claims.
sources.does_not_prove: That every wealthy household gained or every poorer household lost; these are group averages.

sources.title: Poverty risk in Germany 2025
supports: 13.3 million people, or 16.1%, were at risk of poverty.
The threshold for a single person was €1,446 net per month.
21.2% were at risk of poverty or social exclusion.
sources.does_not_prove: That everyone below the relative threshold experiences the same material deprivation.

sources.title: Poverty risk by household type
sources.exact_location: 2025 column · household type table · updated 9 April 2026
supports: 30.3% of single-person households were at risk of poverty.
28.9% of single-parent households were at risk of poverty.
sources.does_not_prove: That household type itself causes poverty.

sources.title: Living conditions — unexpected expenses
sources.exact_location: Germany · 2025 · inability to face unexpected financial expenses
supports: 31.9% of people in Germany were recorded as unable to face unexpected financial expenses.
sources.does_not_prove: The size of an individual's wealth or the reason for their financial vulnerability.

sources.title: Federal budget 2026
sources.source_type: Enacted federal budget / digital budget view
supports: The Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs budget is €197.341 billion, 37.62% of the federal budget.
sources.does_not_prove: That all BMAS spending goes to low-income households; substantial spending is social-insurance and life-cycle redistribution.

sources.title: 30th Federal Subsidy Report
supports: Reported federal subsidy volume rises to an estimated €77.8 billion in 2026.
sources.does_not_prove: That the subsidy envelope is wasteful, removable, or captured by wealthy households; individual measures have different goals and beneficiaries.

sources.title: Participation benefit take-up
sources.authority: Research analysis using administrative/official benefit context
sources.exact_location: 2026 analysis · participation benefit take-up by age
supports: Only around 18% of eligible 6-to-under-15-year-olds and 12% of 15-to-under-18-year-olds in the analysed groups received the participation benefit.
sources.does_not_prove: A general non-take-up rate for Bürgergeld, Wohngeld or every German social benefit.

sources.title: Social-benefit reform microsimulations
sources.exact_location: 1 June 2026 · reform comparison for housing benefit, child supplement and basic income support
supports: IAB and ifo modelled alternative combinations of housing benefit, child supplement and basic income support, showing that design choices change fiscal costs and work incentives.
sources.does_not_prove: That one reform is universally optimal; distribution, incentives and fiscal effects depend on the design.
